subs.text: One three-digit number can decide whether you get the apartment, and how much interest you pay on a car or a home.
That number is your credit score.
Most people have no idea how it's actually calculated.
In the next few minutes, you will.
Most lenders in the US use the FICO score, and it runs from 300 to 850.
Below 580 is poor. 580 to 669 is fair.
670 to 739 is good. 740 to 799 is very good.
And 800 or higher is exceptional.
Your score is built from five ingredients.
And they are not equal.
The biggest one, about 35 percent, is payment history.
Do you pay on time?
A payment that's 30 or more days late can be reported to the credit bureaus, and stay on your report for up to seven years.
The simplest fix: set up autopay for at least the minimum on every card.
Next, about 30 percent, is how much you owe, mainly your credit utilization.
That's your card balances divided by your total credit limits.
If your limit is 5,000 dollars and your balance is 2,500, your utilization is 50 percent. That looks risky.
Common advice is to stay under 30 percent. People with the highest scores often stay under 10.
About 15 percent is the length of your credit history.
Older accounts help.
That's why closing your oldest credit card can actually lower your score.
The last two are about 10 percent each.
New credit: every application can trigger a hard inquiry, which may cost you a few points for a while.
And credit mix: having different types, like a card and a loan, helps a little. But never take a loan just for this.
One myth to kill right now.
Checking your own score does not hurt it. That's a soft inquiry.
You can get your reports from all three bureaus for free at annualcreditreport.com.
So, to recap.
Pay on time. Keep balances low. Keep old accounts open. And apply for new credit only when you need it.
Do those four things consistently, and your score takes care of itself.
In the next video, we'll show how to raise your score fast. Subscribe so you don't miss it.
